basic_information.name: Foundation Model Governance (Cross-Jurisdictional Issue Area)
basic_information.status: Partially in_force (EU GPAI rules Aug 2025), partially enacted (California SB 53 Jan 2026), partially voluntary (Seoul Commitments, G7 Hiroshima Code)
basic_information.effective_date: EU GPAI obligations: 2 August 2025; EU enforcement powers: 2 August 2026; California SB 53: 1 January 2026; G7 Hiroshima Code: October 2023 (voluntary); Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments: May 2024 (voluntary); UK AISI evaluations: ongoing since November 2023
basic_information.regulatory_philosophy: Varies by jurisdiction: comprehensive_horizontal (EU AI Act GPAI tier), patchwork_federalism with innovation_first_light_touch (US federal under Trump, state-level SB 53 in California), sector_specific voluntary (UK pro-innovation approach with AISI evaluations), state_control (China mandatory algorithm registration and content labeling), voluntary_principles (G7 Hiroshima Process, Seoul Commitments, Frontier Model Forum)

scope_and_content.summary: Foundation model governance addresses the specific rules, safety testing requirements, incident reporting obligations, and transparency mandates that apply to the most capable general-purpose AI models (also called frontier models). The EU AI Act creates a two-tier system for GPAI models: all providers above 10^23 FLOPs must meet transparency and copyright obligations, while models above 10^25 FLOPs (systemic risk) face additional safety evaluation, adversarial testing, cybersecurity, and incident reporting requirements. California SB 53 targets frontier models above 10^26 FLOPs with safety framework publication and incident reporting. Internationally, the G7 Hiroshima Process and Seoul Summit Frontier AI Safety Commitments establish voluntary codes of conduct for organizations developing the most advanced AI systems.
key_provisions: EU AI Act Article 53 — All GPAI model providers must: (a) maintain technical documentation, (b) provide information to downstream AI system providers, (c) comply with EU copyright law including text and data mining opt-out obligations, (d) publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training data content

EU AI Act Article 51 — GPAI models trained with cumulative compute >10^25 FLOPs are presumed to pose systemic risk; providers must notify the Commission within 2 weeks of meeting/foreseeing this threshold; providers may contest classification with robust counter-evidence

EU AI Act Article 55 — Systemic risk GPAI providers must: (a) perform state-of-the-art model evaluations via standardized protocols (benchmarks, red teaming, human uplift studies), (b) assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level, (c) track, document, and report serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, (d) ensure adequate cybersecurity for model and physical infrastructure

GPAI Code of Practice (July 2025) — Three chapters: (1) Transparency, (2) Copyright, (3) Safety & Security; signatories benefit from 'presumption of conformity' safe harbor; Safety chapter requires cutting-edge Safety and Security Framework before model release, covering evaluation triggers, risk categories, mitigation strategies, forecasting methods, and organizational responsibilities

California SB 53 (TFAIA) — Frontier developers (models >10^26 FLOPs) must: (a) publish accessible safety framework incorporating national/international standards and catastrophic risk assessment, (b) report critical safety incidents to Office of Emergency Services within 15 days (24 hours if imminent risk of death/serious injury), (c) publish transparency reports at model launch, (d) provide whistleblower protections with anonymous internal reporting platform

G7 Hiroshima Process (October 2023) — 11 guiding principles and voluntary Code of Conduct for organizations developing advanced AI, including: pre-deployment safety testing, red teaming, information sharing on capabilities and risks, cybersecurity investment, content provenance mechanisms, public reporting of capabilities and limitations

Seoul Frontier AI Safety Commitments (May 2024) — 20 organizations (including Anthropic, Microsoft, NVIDIA, OpenAI) committed to: publishing safety frameworks, internal/external red-teaming for severe/novel threats, cybersecurity and insider threat safeguards, third-party vulnerability discovery, prioritizing societal risk research

UK AI Security Institute (AISI) — Conducts voluntary pre-deployment evaluations of frontier AI systems across national security and public safety domains; has evaluated 30+ frontier systems since November 2023; no binding legal mandate but operates through voluntary agreements with developers

China — Mandatory algorithm registration with CAC for generative AI services with public opinion/social mobilization capabilities; mandatory filing of LLMs; content labeling requirements (effective September 2025) for AI-generated/synthetic content; national security assessments for foundation models before public deployment
scope_and_content.risk_classification: EU AI Act creates a two-tier GPAI classification: (1) Standard GPAI models (>10^23 FLOPs) with transparency and copyright obligations, and (2) GPAI models with systemic risk (>10^25 FLOPs) with additional safety evaluation, adversarial testing, incident reporting, and cybersecurity requirements. California SB 53 uses a higher threshold (>10^26 FLOPs) to define 'frontier models.' The Hiroshima Process and Seoul Commitments use qualitative criteria ('most advanced AI systems,' 'frontier models') without a specific compute threshold. China does not use compute thresholds but requires registration for all generative AI services with public-facing capabilities.
scope_and_content.covered_entities: EU: providers of GPAI models placed on the EU market (regardless of where headquartered); California SB 53: frontier developers and 'large frontier developers' (annual revenue >$500M, approximately 5-8 companies currently); G7/Seoul: voluntary signatories (major AI labs); UK AISI: voluntary participants; China: all domestic providers of generative AI and algorithm-based services
scope_and_content.sector_scope: Cross-sector — foundation model governance applies horizontally across all sectors where GPAI models are deployed. EU AI Act GPAI rules apply regardless of downstream use case. SB 53 focuses specifically on model developers, not deployers. China's rules apply to all internet-facing generative AI services. Military/national security uses are generally excluded from EU AI Act but not from national security-related evaluations by UK AISI.
scope_and_content.open_source_treatment: EU AI Act Article 53(2) provides exemptions for open-source GPAI models meeting three conditions: (1) released under a free and open-source license allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution, (2) model parameters/weights/architecture publicly available, (3) not monetized. Exempt providers skip technical documentation and downstream provider information obligations but MUST still comply with copyright/training data summary requirements. CRITICAL EXCEPTION: open-source models classified as systemic risk (>10^25 FLOPs) receive NO exemptions — all Article 55 obligations apply regardless of open-source status. The GPAI Code of Practice offers simplified compliance pathways for SMEs. California SB 53 makes no open-source distinction — any model above 10^26 FLOPs is covered regardless of license.
scope_and_content.extraterritorial_reach: EU AI Act applies to all GPAI model providers placing models on the EU market, regardless of headquarters location — non-EU providers must appoint an EU-based authorized representative (except open-source exempt providers). This means US companies like OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Anthropic must comply with EU GPAI rules for models available in Europe. California SB 53 applies to any developer training frontier models, with enforcement by the California Attorney General. The G7 Hiroshima Process is voluntary but aims for global reach through OECD reporting framework (49 countries). China's regulations apply to services available to Chinese users.

compliance_and_enforcement.penalties: EU AI Act: fines up to 3% of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million (whichever is higher) for GPAI-specific violations; up to 7% or EUR 35 million for prohibited practices. California SB 53: civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per violation, enforced by California Attorney General; attorney's fees awarded to successful whistleblower plaintiffs. China: penalties include service suspension, fines, and potential criminal liability for serious violations. G7/Seoul/UK AISI: no binding penalties (voluntary frameworks).
compliance_and_enforcement.enforcement_body: EU: AI Office (within European Commission), operational since August 2025, responsible for GPAI model enforcement. California: California Attorney General and Office of Emergency Services (for incident reports). China: Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR). UK: AI Security Institute (AISI) conducts evaluations; no dedicated AI regulatory body — sector regulators maintain oversight. G7/OECD: no enforcement body; OECD facilitates voluntary reporting.
compliance_and_enforcement.compliance_timeline: EU GPAI obligations: effective 2 August 2025 for new models; enforcement powers (fines) from 2 August 2026; legacy models (placed on market before Aug 2025) must comply by 2 August 2027; member states must establish AI regulatory sandboxes by 2 August 2026. California SB 53: effective 1 January 2026; large frontier developers must publish safety frameworks by January 2026. G7 Hiroshima reporting: first round of reports due 15 April 2025. Seoul Commitments: safety frameworks to be published within a year of signing (by May 2025). China content labeling: effective 1 September 2025.
compliance_and_enforcement.reporting_requirements: EU Article 55: providers of systemic risk GPAI must track, document, and report serious incidents to the AI Office 'without undue delay,' plus report possible corrective measures. EU Article 53: all GPAI providers must publish training data summaries and maintain technical documentation accessible to regulators. California SB 53: report critical safety incidents to OES within 15 days (24 hours for imminent death/injury risk); publish transparency reports at model launch; large frontier developers must publish safety frameworks. G7 Hiroshima: voluntary reporting via OECD framework. China: mandatory algorithm filing, LLM filing, and security assessments before public deployment.
compliance_and_enforcement.sme_provisions: EU AI Act explicitly requires the GPAI Code of Practice to allow 'simplified ways of compliance for SMEs, including start-ups, in order not to represent an excessive cost.' Specific provisions: (1) reduced training data disclosure — SMEs report top 5% of internet domains crawled (vs. 10% for large companies), (2) AI regulatory sandboxes must be established in each member state by August 2026 with priority access for SMEs/startups, (3) open-source exemption from documentation obligations reduces burden for small open-source model providers. California SB 53 implicitly protects smaller companies through its high 10^26 FLOPs threshold, which currently covers only 5-8 companies; additionally, only 'large frontier developers' (>$500M revenue) face the full set of obligations.
compliance_and_enforcement.liability_model: EU: The AI Liability Directive proposal was WITHDRAWN by the European Commission in February 2025. Instead, the revised Product Liability Directive (member state transposition deadline: 9 December 2026) extends strict product liability to software including AI systems — developers/providers are treated as manufacturers, liable without requiring proof of negligence. For GPAI models specifically, the AI Act establishes regulatory compliance obligations but does not create a direct private right of action. California SB 53: no private right of action for general violations, but whistleblower plaintiffs can recover attorney's fees; enforcement is through AG civil penalties. Overall: fault_based in most jurisdictions, with product_liability (strict) emerging in EU for defective AI products.

impact_and_analysis.business_impact: Foundation model governance creates highly asymmetric impacts across company sizes: (1) LARGE LABS (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral): face the heaviest obligations — EU systemic risk compliance (Article 55), California SB 53 full requirements, Seoul Commitments — requiring dedicated safety teams, red-teaming infrastructure, incident response systems, and legal/compliance staff across multiple jurisdictions; estimated compliance costs in millions of dollars annually. (2) MID-TIER MODEL PROVIDERS: face EU Article 53 transparency/documentation obligations if models exceed 10^23 FLOPs, but likely fall below systemic risk threshold — compliance is manageable but requires documentation infrastructure and copyright compliance processes. (3) STARTUPS AND SMEs: largely shielded by high compute thresholds and open-source exemptions; can leverage open-source models (Llama, Mistral 7B) to avoid GPAI provider obligations entirely; regulatory sandboxes provide testing environments; however, startups building on top of GPAI models may face downstream deployer obligations. (4) EUROPEAN vs. US COMPANIES: European AI companies (notably Mistral) face a dual challenge — compliance costs from EU GPAI rules while competing against US companies operating under lighter federal regulation; 56 EU-based AI companies signed a July 2025 letter warning compliance costs could stifle innovation. (5) OPEN-SOURCE ECOSYSTEM: EU open-source exemptions preserve the ability to release models freely, but systemic risk models (>10^25 FLOPs) like Llama receive no exemption, potentially chilling open release of the most capable models.
impact_and_analysis.innovation_effect: Mixed and contested. CONSTRAINING FACTORS: EU GPAI obligations add compliance overhead that may disadvantage European model developers; the 'stop the clock' campaign by 56 EU companies (including Mistral, Aleph Alpha) argued for a 2-year delay, suggesting innovation friction. Stanford's 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index found overall transparency declining (average 40.69/100), with copyright litigation actively disincentivizing training data disclosure. PROMOTING FACTORS: The GPAI Code of Practice's 'presumption of conformity' provides legal certainty that may encourage investment; regulatory sandboxes create safe experimentation spaces; open-source exemptions preserve innovation pathways for smaller players; the EU's approach may create a 'race to the top' on safety, building consumer trust. The US under Trump is explicitly pursuing deregulation to maintain AI dominance, creating a regulatory arbitrage opportunity. California SB 53's focus on the largest models (10^26 FLOPs) limits innovation impact to a handful of frontier labs.
impact_and_analysis.global_influence: Strong 'Brussels effect' dynamics: EU GPAI rules are becoming the de facto global standard since major AI companies must comply to access the EU market. The GPAI Code of Practice is described as 'the world's first guidance for GPAI model compliance.' California SB 53 extends EU-style requirements to the US context for the first time. The G7 Hiroshima Process (49 countries) and Seoul Commitments (20 organizations) create multilateral alignment around similar principles. UK AISI has inspired a global network of AI Safety Institutes (US, Japan, Singapore, Canada, France, Korea). China's approach — mandatory registration with pre-deployment security reviews — represents an alternative governance model emphasizing state control over content and capabilities. The compute-threshold approach (10^23, 10^25, 10^26 FLOPs) pioneered by the EU and adopted by California is becoming an emerging global standard for scoping foundation model regulation.
impact_and_analysis.stakeholder_positions: INDUSTRY (split): Major AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft) signed Seoul Commitments and largely accept GPAI framework — Mistral and OpenAI publicly backed EU GPAI Code of Practice in July 2025. However, 56 EU companies lobbied to delay implementation. Mistral AI and Aleph Alpha earlier lobbied to shift EU rules to focus on applications rather than models. CIVIL SOCIETY: Corporate Europe Observatory documented how European startups 'teamed up with Big Tech to gut the AI Act'; AI safety organizations (METR, CSET Georgetown) generally support robust evaluation requirements. GOVERNMENTS: France backed lighter GPAI rules (supporting Mistral), while other EU members pushed for stronger obligations; US under Trump prioritizes deregulation and innovation; UK maintains voluntary pro-innovation approach. ACADEMIA: Stanford HAI transparency research shows companies are becoming less transparent despite growing regulation; CSET Georgetown called the EU Code of Practice a potential 'new global standard' for AI safety.
impact_and_analysis.deregulatory_signals: US (federal): Trump revoked Biden's EO 14110 (January 2025), explicitly pursuing 'minimally burdensome' AI framework; December 2025 EO seeks federal preemption of state AI laws. EU: Commission rejected the 'stop the clock' campaign but withdrew the AI Liability Directive (February 2025), signaling pragmatism on enforcement; the GPAI Code of Practice is voluntary (though creates presumption of conformity). UK: explicitly chose not to create new AI legislation, relying on sector regulators and voluntary AISI evaluations. Japan and India maintain innovation-first approaches with minimal binding requirements for foundation models.

teaching_relevance.entrepreneurial_implications: Foundation model governance is critical for AI entrepreneurs at every stage: (1) BUILD vs. BUY DECISION: Startups using open-source models below 10^25 FLOPs as deployers avoid GPAI provider obligations, while those training custom large models face significant compliance costs — this fundamentally shapes the build-vs-buy calculus. (2) MARKET ACCESS: EU GPAI compliance is effectively mandatory for accessing the 450M-consumer EU market; entrepreneurs must budget for documentation, training data summaries, and potential copyright compliance from day one. (3) COMPLIANCE COST ASYMMETRY: The regulatory landscape strongly favors application-layer startups over model-training startups — estimated compliance costs for systemic risk models run into millions annually (safety teams, red-teaming, legal), while downstream deployers face lighter obligations. (4) OPEN-SOURCE STRATEGY: The EU open-source exemption creates a viable path for startups to release models without full GPAI compliance, but this exemption vanishes at systemic risk scale — entrepreneurs must plan their scaling trajectory with this cliff in mind. (5) GEOGRAPHIC ARBITRAGE: US federal deregulation under Trump vs. EU comprehensive regulation creates strategic choices about where to headquarter and which markets to prioritize; California SB 53 complicates the US picture. (6) SANDBOX OPPORTUNITIES: EU regulatory sandboxes (mandatory in each member state by August 2026) offer startups controlled environments to test AI products with reduced compliance burden. (7) COMPETITIVE MOATS: Early compliance with GPAI rules can become a competitive advantage — 'presumption of conformity' from Code of Practice adherence provides legal certainty that non-compliant competitors lack. (8) TRANSPARENCY AS DIFFERENTIATOR: With Stanford showing average transparency at 40.69/100, startups that voluntarily exceed transparency requirements may build trust advantages.
teaching_relevance.session_mapping: Session 5 (Ethics, governance & final presentations) — primary; Session 3 (Framing & managing AI projects) — secondary (build-vs-buy implications, GPAI compliance in project planning); Session 4 (AI business models & strategy) — secondary (regulatory compliance costs, geographic strategy, competitive moats from safety)

caveats: EU GPAI enforcement is in its earliest phase — the AI Office is taking a collaborative approach in year one (2025-2026), and actual enforcement patterns remain to be established
The 10^25 FLOPs threshold for systemic risk is acknowledged as a rough proxy; the Commission may adjust or supplement it as the field evolves
Trump's December 2025 EO seeking federal preemption of state AI laws could potentially conflict with California SB 53 — legal challenges are likely but unresolved as of February 2026
The AI Liability Directive withdrawal leaves a gap in EU AI liability framework — the Product Liability Directive covers products but not services, creating potential gaps for AI-as-a-service
China's regulatory landscape is evolving rapidly with multiple overlapping measures; exact enforcement patterns are less transparent than EU/US
The voluntary nature of G7/Seoul/UK commitments means compliance varies significantly across signatories — METR tracks actual implementation
Compute thresholds will become outdated as training efficiency improves — a model with equivalent capabilities may be trained below thresholds in future
The GPAI Code of Practice provides 'presumption of conformity' but this has not yet been tested in enforcement proceedings
